title: Holy Family
logline: The week after Christmas on Glenwood Avenue: a television show nobody in the family can stop watching, a father at a bolted table, a phone call at an hour nobody keeps — and midnight three times.

s01.slug: SATURDAY · 10:40 AM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE DRIVEWAY
body: The flat shovel goes down the drive with a scrape that carries to the end of the block, and what it’s after is the slush from Christmas, gone hard in the tire tracks into two gray ribbons that don’t want to come up. Jack gets the edge under one and leans on the handle until a slab breaks loose, carries it to the bank by the garage, and comes back for the next. Two streets over a plow is working toward Midlothian: the blade comes down on the pavement with a bang, scrapes the length of a house, lifts, and bangs down again. Up and down Glenwood the cans are out at the curb with Christmas standing up out of them — red paper and gold paper and plaid, a flattened box that held somebody’s new television, tissue by the armload — and the lids balanced on top.

His father comes down behind him in the Browns knit with a bag of rock salt on his hip and a Dixie cup out of the bathroom dispenser for a scoop. He dips it and throws from the wrist, short and flat, and the salt goes out over the concrete in a fan and rattles on the ice, and he dips again. He doesn’t waste any. His ears are red under the edge of the knit. In the front window Rosie is watching the two of them with the blue crab under her arm.

The new snow brush hangs off the Silverado’s side mirror by its strap with the tag still on it, where Frank put it Christmas morning, because the old one, the one held together with electrical tape, still works. They do the drive from the garage down, Jack breaking and Frank salting behind him, and they don’t talk, and it isn’t the kind of not talking that needs fixing. A woman goes by on the sidewalk with a dog in a sweater and says *Merry Christmas, Frank*, and Frank says it back with his eyes on the ice, and the dog stops to consider the salt and is talked out of it.
The phone has been going off in the Carhartt since breakfast. At the bottom of the drive Jack stands the shovel up on its blade, leans on it, and reads them in the order they came.

Tomorrow is the twenty-seventh. Since Christmas the date hasn’t come up in the house.
Frank has stopped a few feet up the drive with the cup full. He says it to the salt in it, not to Jack.
“What’s it like. In there. Now.”

Jack was in it last Sunday with his mother, and again on Thursday with Theo. On the next street the plow bangs down and scrapes off toward the corner, and the quiet comes back in behind it. He puts the phone in his pocket.

body: By ten past two the light is already leaving the front window, the sky over the roofs across Glenwood going from gray to grayer without bothering with anything in between, and the tree is lit against it anyway, every bulb. Gina comes down the stairs with the box set held flat against her chest — his Christmas present, in her room since Christmas night — and kneels in front of the TV and feeds it disc one.
“For research,” she says. She skips the first three episodes from the menu without consulting anybody. “Setup. The regatta’s the one.”

The family arrives by accident, one at a time. Nonna is already in her chair by the window under Theo’s cashmere, with her beads. Rosie comes in and lies down on her stomach on the rug with the blue crab under her chin. Ma comes in from the kitchen with a dish towel to fold and stands behind the couch folding it, and ten minutes later she is still folding the same towel. Frank appears in the kitchen doorway with his coffee, just seeing, and comes no farther.
“Is this the boat one?”
“That’s her *Facebook*, Dad,” Gina says.

*Sweetwater* opens on a lake: long and gray, with mountains standing up behind it that Gina says are really Canada, and a boathouse, and a dock, and a line of girls in navy blazers going down it two by two with oars on their shoulders. It’s regatta weekend. Parents are arriving in good cars. A cello is doing most of the work.
And there she is, coming down the boathouse stairs with a clipboard against her chest, the smallest girl on the dock, the one who steers, and Nonna’s hand comes up off the beads. “*L’attrice!*”

She’s eighteen in it. Her hair is darker and ironed straight, the freckles are gone under somebody’s foundation, and the blazer is buttoned to the top. It’s the girl from the window seat in Montecito, and she is doing something Jack has never seen her do, which is hold still.

A rower comes up the dock to carry the clipboard for her. His name is Reid, and he has a jaw like a mailbox. When he makes a joke, Cassidy laughs at it, and it’s the laugh she gives strangers who raise a phone at her in a parking lot — bright, quick, all teeth — and Jack, on the end of the couch, knows it from the real one from across the front room.
“Is that really a school?” Rosie says.
“It’s *Canada*, Rosie.”
By the end of the first act Reid has kissed her at the end of the dock at sunset, carefully, the cello going like it’s being paid by the hour.
Every time she comes back on after that — the dining hall, the stairs, a dormitory window with the lake in it — Nonna announces her. “*L’attrice.*” “We *know*, Nonna,” Gina says, every time.

Cassidy’s mother arrives in the second act. She is blond and tan and beautifully dressed, and at a restaurant in town with white tablecloths, with the rest of the crew team’s parents at the next table, she takes Cassidy’s hand across the bread basket and tells her, smiling, in a voice nobody else at the table can hear, that she was such a sweet little girl, and it was so much easier to love her then.

Cassidy keeps smiling through all of it. That’s the thing Jack watches: the smile stays exactly where it is, polite, for the parents at the next table, while everything above it goes out like a porch light. He has watched her do the reverse of that since November — the eyes going on while the mouth stays put — and it’s the same muscle, run backward.
Behind the couch Ma stops folding. “*Disgraziata*,” Ma says under her breath — a word she does not use in front of Rosie, and has just used in front of Rosie.

In the chair by the window the rosary comes up in Nonna’s fist. “*Povera*,” Nonna says, and her lips go to work on the beads, fast, in Calabrese, praying for the girl at the table, and she doesn’t stop till the scene does.
Before the race Cassidy goes into the school chapel by herself and lights a candle and doesn’t pray, just looks at it with the clipboard in her lap.
Nonna nods at the candle, approving of it.
“She’s nice,” Rosie says.

The girl who ruins it is named Whitney. She has red hair and a lacrosse stick she carries everywhere for reasons the show doesn’t go into, and the morning of the race she tells the coach something about Cassidy that isn’t true, and the coach takes Cassidy out of the boat and puts Whitney in, and Sweetwater comes in third behind two schools Gina says don’t count. “And Sweetwater is *not* in the boat,” Gina says, low, like the man who does the golf. At the finish line the camera finds Cassidy alone on the shore with her clipboard against her chest and the wind in her hair, being brave about it in a way that makes Rosie put the crab over her own face.
“*Cassidy*,” Nonna says, to her, with feeling.
That night Whitney finds her on the dock in the dark, crying, and Rosie sits up on the rug with the crab.
“She doesn’t drown, Rosie,” Gina says. “It’s the *other* one who drowns.”
“Which other one?”
“*That* one. In the spring.”
Rosie lies back down, unsatisfied.

Whitney says she’s sorry. And the camera goes in on Cassidy and stays there, no cello, no anything, while she decides. You can see the mean thing come up into her face — her mother’s thing, the one she could say and be right — and you can see her not say it. It goes out of her a piece at a time, the jaw first and then the mouth, and what’s left is a girl deciding to be kind to somebody who hasn’t earned it, and knowing she hasn’t, and sitting down on the dock beside her anyway.
Jack has seen that face once for real, at one in the morning, in a car, over something smaller, with no camera anywhere.
She’s good. He sits forward on the end of the couch with his elbows on his knees, proud of her in a way he has no right to yet, in front of his entire family, who are doing color commentary.
From the kitchen doorway his father gives his first review of a television program in Jack’s memory. “She’s good.”
Ma, folding again: “Which one is she really, Jack? This one, or the boat?”

response: “Neither,” Jack says. “She’s better than both.”
“Better how?” Ma says.
He opens his mouth to tell her, and over by the window Nonna’s beads are still going, and he can’t do it with them going.
“Oh my *God*,” Gina says, into a cushion.

choices.text: “Cassidy. Nobody fakes a blazer like that.”
response: “Cassidy,” Jack says. “Nobody fakes a blazer like that.”
In the doorway his father laughs, a real one, with coffee in his hand, and has to hold the cup out away from himself till it’s over.
“*Francis*,” Ma says.

He doesn’t answer her. On the screen Cassidy is still sitting on the dock with the girl who doesn’t deserve it, and he watches it to the end: the two of them not talking, the lake going black behind them, the dock lights coming on one after another down the water.
When he looks up, his mother is watching him instead of the television, and her hands have gone still.

s04.slug: SUNDAY · 8:00 AM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE
body: The wreath is gone. Where it stood, somebody from the Altar Society has put up a tree in a bucket wrapped in gold foil, white lights only, and under it the crèche, the straw working loose onto the marble steps. Father Dom is in white. The light off the snow comes in low through the east windows and doesn’t get far, and the tree does the rest. They take the pew they always take: Nonna on the aisle with her beads, then Rosie, Ma, Jack, Gina, and Frank on the end in his one sport coat, with his hat on his knee.

The second reading is Mrs. Dulik, who runs the bingo, in a red blazer with a poinsettia pin. *Put on, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.* She reads it at bingo speed, as if somebody might not be listening, and stops at *giving thanks to God the Father through him* — one verse short of the wives — and closes the book on her finger and goes back to her pew.

Father Dom reads the Gospel with a cough drop parked in his cheek. Luke: the boy at twelve, and the caravan a day down the road before anybody counts heads; three days of going back the way they came; and the boy in the Temple the entire time, sitting among the teachers, asking them questions. *Son, why have you done this to us? Your father and I have been looking for you with great anxiety.* The answer he gives her isn’t one she can use. *And his mother kept all these things in her heart.*
He takes the ambo with both hands and puts his weight on the good knee.

“My mother lost me at Idora Park in 1953,” he says. “Three hours. My father walked every inch of that park twice in his work shoes. You know where they found me? In line for the Wildcat. Third time.” A sound goes along the pews from the people old enough to have ridden it. “I wasn’t lost. I knew right where I was. It was them didn’t know.” He moves the cough drop over. “That’s the Holy Family. Not the Christmas card. Two people walking back the way they came, looking in every face. And when they find him she doesn’t understand a word he says to her. And she keeps it anyway.”
He looks out at them over his glasses a second, and sits down.
On the steps after, Frank goes on ahead with the keys already out, and Jack opens the RAZR under the overhang where the salt is thickest.

s05.slug: SUNDAY · 9:50 AM · TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION, THE LOT
body: On the radio a caller from Parma is explaining that two in a row is how they get you, every year: they win two in December and you go and buy season tickets like an idiot. The host says *sir* and *sir* and goes to a commercial for a furniture store in Mentor that is having the biggest sale in its history. Frank has the last row again, nose to the fence, where the plows have shoved the snow up along the chain-link in a gray bank as high as the grille. The engine is running. The heater is running.

Gina is already out, stamping her boots on the salt. Rosie is out with her in her church coat with the velvet collar, holding Gina’s sleeve and looking up at the wire that runs along the top of the fence, and through the glass Jack hears her ask Gina: “Is Pop staying with the truck again?” Gina pulls her hood up for her. “Shh.”
Ma has the Folgers can of quarters in her lap. She has been shaking it a little, to hear what’s in it, since the church lot.
From the back seat Jack can see the back of his father’s neck, shaved close this morning and nicked under the ear, and the gray coming in under the edge of the Browns hat.
Frank has both hands on the wheel. Under his open work coat the sport coat is still on, from church.
The dashboard clock says 9:51. Ma gets out and stands in her open door with the can against her hip, and leans back in across the seat to him.
“He said Pop too,” she says. “He said tell him he said.”
The furniture store in Mentor wants everybody to know they’ll beat any price. Frank’s thumbs are on top of the wheel. He doesn’t look at her, or at Jack. He looks at the building.

response: “He asked for you, Dad.”
Frank keeps looking at the building a long time: the yellow brick, the windows that are slots, the flag over the entrance standing straight out in the wind off the fields.
“I know when they kick off.”
Outside, Gina knocks on Jack’s window with one knuckle and points at her wrist, where she isn’t wearing a watch.

choices.text: *Get out. Stand at his window and wait.*
response: Jack gets out and walks around the hood and stands at the driver’s door with his hands in the Carhartt. The wind comes across the lot off the fields and finds the gap in his collar.

Frank doesn’t look at him. Inside the cab the call-in show has come back from the furniture store and gone on about Oakland: the run defense, the long flight, what a West Coast trip does to a team in December.

body: Frank turns the key.

The radio quits in the middle of a man’s sentence — *the thing about Oakland is* — and the fan winds down, and the cab is quiet enough to hear the wind in the fence. He takes the Browns hat off and folds it in half and puts it inside his coat, against the sport coat. He gets out and comes around the back of the truck and follows Ma across the lot, with Gina and Rosie and Jack strung out behind him on the salt.

The lobby is the lobby — the yellow cinderblock, the mural of the sun with a face, the ducks — except that the Sunday after Christmas every plastic chair in it is taken, and a boy in new light-up sneakers is stamping a slow circle on the tile to make them go. The officer at the desk says, “Maria,” and she says his name back, and he looks past her at the man in the sport coat, and runs a finger down the list on his clipboard, and stops it.
“Costigan, Francis.”
“Yes sir,” Frank says, and slides his license across, and signs the visitor log under Ma’s name in capitals, pressing hard enough to go through to the page underneath.

Coats in the lockers; phones in the lockers. Jack puts the RAZR on the shelf beside Gina’s and shuts the little door on both. The stamp goes on the back of each hand. Frank holds his arm out straight and looks off at the ducks on the mural, like a man getting a shot.

The first steel door opens, and they go through, and it shuts behind them before the second one will open. In the space between, with the cinderblock close on both sides and nothing to look at, Frank says it to Ma, low, so the girls won’t hear.
“Where do I stand?”
Ma doesn’t turn around.
“You sit, Frank,” she says. “You sit with him.”
The second door opens.

s05b.slug: SUNDAY · 10:10 AM · TRUMBULL, THE VISITING ROOM
body: The paper tree is still taped up over the microwave, but the tape has given out at one corner, and the top of it hangs forward over the room. At the next table two grandmothers in church hats are splitting a clementine section by section and passing the peel back and forth in a little pile. A girl in a red Christmas dress is asleep across two of the bolted chairs with somebody’s coat over her legs, and at the table under the platform a boy is showing his father something on a new Nintendo, the father bent over it, nodding at every level. Danny has come through the far door ahead of them and is already sitting at the table the officer points them to, in the state blues, with his hands folded on the bolted top. He sees Ma, and Gina, and Rosie, and Jack. Then he sees who is behind Ma, and stands up, his hands still folded in front of him, as if the Gospel is starting.
Up on the platform the officer says, “Costigan,” not loud.
Danny sits. He watches his father come the rest of the way to the table, a step behind Ma, past the boy with the Nintendo and the sleeping girl, in the sport coat, with his hands at his sides.

Ma bends and kisses the top of his head, the inside haircut, and sits down next to him and takes a stack of paper napkins out of her purse, brought from home, and deals one to each place as if it’s the kitchen table. Frank sits across from his son, in a bolted chair built for somebody shorter, with his knees up against the underside of the table. He puts his hands in his lap, under the table, and Ma reaches over and takes him by the wrist and brings them up and sets them on the bolted top, where the platform can see them, and leaves her hand there.
“They play Oakland at four,” Frank says.
“They’ll lose.”
“They won’t.”
Danny looks at his father. Frank looks at the paper tree.

Gina has done the first run to the machines with a fistful of Ma’s quarters, and comes back with honey buns in their cellophane and puts one down in front of everybody. Frank says he’s fine. Ma pushes it over to him anyway. Rosie folds her hands on the table and checks with Ma, and Ma nods.
“Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts,” Rosie says, fast, the way she practiced it in the bathroom mirror for a week, “and Danny, and Nonna’s hand, and for Pop, who came. Amen.”
“Amen,” Danny says. “You get that off the rich one?”
“I got it off the *mirror*,” Rosie says.
The table eats.
“Nonna get her slippers?” Danny says.
“She wears them over her shoes,” Gina says. “To *Mass*.”
Danny nods: correct. “She’s eighty-four. She can wear what she wants over what she wants.”

Gina tells him about the Flip — Theo gave her a camera, she’s making a documentary — and Danny says about what, and Gina says *us*, and Danny says don’t put him in it, and Gina says he’s the DVD extras, and Danny laughs with his mouth full and has to put his hand over it. Three tables over, Reggie from Portsmouth, visiting with the woman in the church hat, lifts his chin at the table, and Danny lifts his back.
“Reggie got everybody on the unit doing ‘Feliz Navidad’ at the chaplain’s Mass,” he tells Rosie. “Badly. On purpose. The chaplain sang it too.”
“Pop fell asleep at Midnight Mass,” Gina says.
“Around Quirinius,” Jack says.
“Everybody falls asleep at Quirinius,” Danny says. “That’s what he’s for.”

“So who ate the eel?” Danny says, with his mouth full. “Me,” Jack says. “First. Pop paid five.” Danny turns all the way around in the bolted chair to look at his father. “Twenty-four years.” “It was a bet,” Frank says.
“I drew the TV girl,” Rosie tells him. “With Jack. And the crab.”
“Yeah? What’s she look like?”
“Yellow hair. And Jack’s holding the crab, because she’s scared of it.”
“Smart girl,” Danny says.
“You drew the TV one?” Danny licks the glaze off his thumb and sits back as far as a bolted chair goes and turns to his brother. He has been saving it since Christmas. It is all over his face.
“So,” he says. “The TV one.”
“She was on a *yacht*,” Gina says.
“Gina says yacht.” Danny tells it to the table. “On the phone it was a boat.”
“It was a *yacht*. It had a *bathroom*.” Gina leans in over the wrappers. “And we watched season two. All of disc one. Pop came in four times. Ma watched every minute.”
“I was folding,” Ma says.
“Ma watched,” Danny says. Ma straightens a napkin that doesn’t need it.
“Pop said she’s good,” Gina says.
Danny turns to his father. “Pop said *good*? Pop don’t say good about the *Browns*.”
Frank reaches for his honey bun.
“And she’s seen him,” Danny says to Gina, past Jack. “In person. His face.”
“She’s *seen* him.”

Danny turns back to Jack and shakes his head at him, slow. “Professor. You get sick on the paddle boats at Mill Creek.” He spreads his hands to the table. “Four months he’s out there. Comes home with the TV one. I got Reggie.” And to Jack: “She know about the paddle boats?” “No.” “Don’t tell her.”
And he laughs till the officer up on the platform lowers his newspaper and looks over.
“*Daniel*,” Ma says.
“She’s nice on TV,” Rosie says.
“That’s what I hear,” Danny says, and wipes his eyes with the heel of his hand.
“What’s her name again?” Gina tells him, and he tries it. “*Sky*-ee. With an E, Gina says.”

body: When it has run down, and Gina has handed Rosie a napkin for the glaze on her chin, Ma leans in over the bolted table to her oldest and says it under the room, where only the two of them and Jack can hear it.
“You knew before me.”
Danny doesn’t pretend. “I know everything, Ma. I got time.”
Ma looks at him. She pats his hand on the table, twice, and stands up with the Folgers can. “Frank. Come on.”

She takes him to the machines. Jack watches them go across the room — his mother with the can in the crook of her arm, his father a step behind her in the sport coat — and at the bank of machines along the far wall she starts in on it: the quarters and how many, the slot on the end one that sticks so you feed it slow, which button is the coffee, where the cup drops, how you wait for the little light. Frank takes his reading glasses out of his breast pocket and bends to the front of the coffee machine and reads it like a contract. Ma feeds the quarters in for him one at a time; the machine spits one back, and she fishes it out of the return and puts it in again, slower, and shows him with her thumb how slow. A little boy in a clip-on tie has come to stand at Frank’s elbow and supervise. When the cup drops, the boy says, “You gotta wait for the light,” and Frank looks down at him over the glasses and says, “So I’m told.” Gina takes Rosie to the toy corner, where somebody’s little brother is driving a plastic fire truck up the cinderblock as high as he can reach.
Which leaves the table, and the wrappers, and Danny, who keeps his voice under the room.
“Rich one get home?”
“They wanded the baccalà at the airport. Ma’s labels got admired by a federal employee.”
Danny laughs into his fist. “Ma’s gonna put that on the fridge.”
He turns his honey-bun wrapper foil side up and squares it to the edge of the table, and leaves it at that.
Danny looks at him across the table, and Jack lets him.

For a little while Danny doesn’t say anything else, and Jack doesn’t either. The grandmothers at the next table have finished the clementine and are folding the peel into a napkin. In the toy corner Gina is sitting cross-legged on the linoleum in her good skirt, holding the fire truck’s ladder up for the little brother while Rosie explains to him how it goes. Somebody’s baby has fallen asleep with a fist in a man’s collar. Up on the platform the officer turns a page of the newspaper and smooths it flat.
Danny’s eyes have gone past Jack, to the far wall. Jack turns in the bolted chair to see.

Frank has a coffee in each hand now, in the paper cups with the playing cards printed around them, and he is standing in front of the creamer button with his chin down, frowning at it, while Ma explains it to him again with one finger.
“Look at him,” Danny says.

Jack looks. When they were kids Danny used to stand at the Silverado’s fender in the driveway while Frank was under the hood, and hand him the wrench before he asked for it. Their father is holding both cups out from his body a little, as if either one might go off.
“Third’s Ma’s Sunday,” Danny says. “You’re still home.”
“Till the ninth.”
“Don’t let him sit in the truck.”

It’s pale. Cream and two sugars: Jack saw him tear the packets at the machine. That’s how Danny took it at fifteen, standing at the kitchen counter before school with his jacket already on. Danny drinks it black now. Jack knows it from the letters.
Danny looks at the cup. He picks it up and drinks some, and then some more.
“It’s good, Pop.”
Frank sits down with his.

For what’s left of the hour they drink their coffees across the table from each other. The girls come back from the toy corner. Ma tells Danny about the eighth stocking on the mantel, THEO in glitter glue still wet on Christmas morning, and Danny laughs and wants to know did the rich one cry, and Gina says *almost*, and Ma says *Regina*. Frank finishes his coffee and holds the empty cup in both hands with the playing cards facing out.

When the officer calls time every table in the room stands up at once, with a sound like a church getting up off the kneelers. There’s a hug allowed at the end. Danny gets Ma first and rocks her a little on her feet; then Jack, a hand on the back of his head; then Gina, who says *ow* and doesn’t let go; then Rosie, up off the linoleum and swung once and set down. Frank puts his hand out across the bolted table.
Danny looks at it. He takes it.
At the far door, with the other men in blue going through ahead of him, Danny turns around and says it to Jack in his normal voice, loud enough for the room.
“Penance is done. You acted normal.”
The officer at the desk looks up from somebody else’s license as they come back through. “Merry Christmas, Frank.”
“Merry Christmas,” Frank says, and gets his coat out of the locker, and puts it on over the sport coat.
Jack gets the RAZR off the shelf and opens it with his own coat still over his arm.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they’d beat Oakland. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over, and didn’t say one other thing about it. Not one. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it.

body: The kickoff comes in off the radio on the workbench from a long way west: a thin crowd in the Oakland Coliseum, a Cleveland man calling it over the hum of the Stroh’s fridge, and down on the concrete the space heater ticking up to orange at Jack’s shins. The colored lights are still strung along the pegboard, one blue bulb still dead in the middle. The Stroh’s fridge is still shut. There is one new thing out here since Christmas. Over the bench, between the pegboard and the Sunoco calendar, the 1964 program hangs in a gallon freezer bag, the Browns and the Colts in their old colors behind the plastic, and the thumbtacks go through the bag at the corners and not through the program.
“You hung it up,” Jack said, coming in.
“Theo said keep it out of the light.”
“It’s in a freezer bag.”
“It’s out of the light,” Frank said, and that was the end of that.

Frank has the bucket, turned over, and the thermos. Jack has the chair with the duct tape on the seat. His father is still in his church shirt, the sport coat hung on a nail by the side door over the snow shovel, and the Browns hat is back on his head where it lives. On Cleveland’s first punt, while the man on the radio follows the ball downfield, Frank says one thing.
“He looks good.”
He says it to the radio. The radio goes to a commercial for a tire place in Elyria.

He spent the Saints game at the kitchen table, mostly, with the RAZR face up beside the plate of leftover struffoli, a thousand miles from the Dome and Lena in her father’s seats, and Ma at the stove asking every time it buzzed who that was. “The Saints.” “The Saints are texting you.” “They’re losing, Ma.” At that she turned around from the sauce and crossed herself for them, on general principle, and turned back. At four he brought the phone out here. Now, with the Browns on and the heater going, he thumbs back to the top of the afternoon and comes down through it, hers and his.

body: The tree is the only light. The house went up at half past ten, Ma last, trying the side door twice, and left the front room to the tree and the furnace and Nonna, who wouldn’t go. She’s asleep in her chair by the window with her head against the wing of it and Theo’s cashmere up under her chin, four feet from where Jack sits on the rug with his back against the couch and *The Moviegoer* open on his knee. She breathes slow and a little loud, in, and then a long time out. The tree puts its colors on the ceiling. Every so often the furnace starts up somewhere under the floor, and the ornaments on the low branches turn a little in the warm air and settle.
At ten past eleven the RAZR goes against his leg. LENA. He has it open before the second buzz, his hand cupped around the bottom of it.
“Hey,” he says, low.

“Hey yourself.” Her voice comes out of the phone full size, a Sunday’s worth of it, and behind it the house on Dupre Street: a television, a cabinet door, Remy saying a linebacker’s name like a curse word. “Why are we whispering?”
“My grandmother’s asleep four feet away.”
On her end a screen door opens on its spring and slaps shut, and the house drops to a murmur behind it. A board creaks, a step taking her weight.
“Then I’ll whisper too,” she whispers.

And she does. He has heard her shout down a seminar, and sing in a basement, and win an argument about a pope at one in the morning. He has never heard her whisper. It turns out to be a different voice altogether, all breath and edges, the New Orleans worn down to the vowels, and it comes from a back step on Dupre Street right up against his ear. He sits very still on his grandmother’s rug and keeps the phone exactly where it is.

“I’m on the back steps in Daddy’s Saints jacket,” she whispers, “and it isn’t even cold out here and I’m freezing, because I’m from here. Daddy hasn’t said a thing since the kick. Remy’s said everything. He blames the defense, the kicker, the Pope, and me, for wearing the wrong earrings. Josie’s got the television up so she doesn’t have to hear either one of them.” The step creaks. “For the record. It was strategy.”
“Overtime was strategy.”
“You don’t peak in December. You peak in February. Sean Payton is resting his *soul*.”
“He looked pretty awake at seventeen–nothing.”
“That’s when he started resting.” The step creaks. “I said a Memorare on the kick. Out loud. Our section heard me. Mr. Thibodeaux behind us took his hat off.”
“And?”
“And He said *wait*.” A breath down the line, all edges. “I hate *wait*. *No* I can argue with.”
He doesn’t say Providence. He’s been told.
“And don’t you argue with me in a whisper, it isn’t fair, I can’t get any volume on it.” A cup set down on wood. “Why is your grandmother asleep in the front room?”
“She won’t go up since Christmas. Ma tried. Pop offered to carry her.” He looks over at the chair. “She says the tree shouldn’t be by itself at night.”
On Dupre Street the step creaks, and for a little there’s only the house behind her, Remy and the television.
“Mémère says that about the dead,” Lena whispers. “You sit up with them.” And then, before it can turn into anything: “Tell her I said she’s right. What page?”
“Ninety-four.”
“Read me something.” And while he’s still turning back toward the tree for the light: “Not Percy. Me.”

So he tips the book to the tree and reads her her own handwriting, as low as he can go and still be heard. Her pencil is small and fast and runs uphill. A *no* on page thirty-one, under something Binx thinks about his secretary. “That stands.” A *ha* on fifty-eight. “That’s a good *ha*. I remember that *ha*.” *Oh, honey*, beside Binx on the Gentilly bus; that one gets nothing from her but the cup picked up off the step, and a drink, and the cup set down.
On page eighty-six, beside Kate, she wrote *spoiled* and underlined it twice.
“Oh, no.”
“Twice.”

“I was seventeen.” Two yards over on Dupre Street a dog barks and quits. “I was seventeen and I was *wrong* about Kate. I thought she was a rich girl having a mood in a nice house. She’s the only person in that house who says out loud she’s in trouble. Everybody else is polishing the silver.”
“Aunt Emily isn’t polishing anything. Aunt Emily’s holding the house up.”
“You *would* take Aunt Emily.”
“You did too.” He turns back to find it in the light, the big speech in the study near the end. “Right here. You wrote *Mémère*.”
What comes down the line would have been a shriek with any air behind it. “Lord have mercy. Don’t you *ever* tell her.”
“Were you wrong?”

“Half.” The step creaks as she settles in to do it properly. “Mémère’s got the silver *and* the rosary. Aunt Emily’s only got the silver. She’s magnificent and she’s wrong. She’s a pagan with good silver. She thinks the world’s going down and all that’s left is to go down like a lady.”
“She’s got a code. She keeps it when it costs her. You always know where the line is with her. Binx doesn’t have a line. Binx has the movies.”

“Binx has a *search*. Aunt Emily quit looking around 1918. A code is what you keep when you’ve stopped expecting anybody to come, Jack. That isn’t faith. That’s beautiful manners at the end of the world.”
“At the end of the world I’d take her over Binx.”
“So would I. In a fight. Not to Mass.”
“Percy gave her the best speech in the book.”
“Percy loves her the way you love the house you grew up in,” Lena says. “And then you move out.”
“Or you stay and fix the roof.”

She laughs the only way a whisper lets you, in short breaths against the phone, and it goes on long enough that he looks over at his grandmother to make sure. Nonna sleeps. The argument doesn’t get scored.
“What’s Binx doing now?” she says. “Where you are.”
“Thinking about his secretary.”
“That’s every page. Don’t you dare read the end first.”
“I never read the end first.”
“Then don’t start with this one. I’ll know. I’ll hear it in your voice.”
“Binx would hate it here,” he says. “Youngstown in December. It’s nothing but everydayness. Salt and the Browns.”
“Binx would *love* it there. Everybody in that town is on the search, Jack. Every man in that bar on Market Street where you watched us lose.” The step creaks. “They just call it the Browns.”

“Tomorrow’s the Innocents,” she whispers. “Mama goes to the seven o’clock every year. Every year since I can remember.” The screen door, very softly, behind her. “I never asked why.” And she goes on to something else before he can say anything: Josie’s science project, which is a volcano, and has been a volcano three years running, and has erupted at one time or another in every room of the house.
“And how was yours?” she says. “Besides the short form.”
Across the rug Nonna breathes in, and out, the long way.

choices.text: “My dad went in today. First time.”
choices.key: Holy Family Sunday, whispering so you wouldn’t wake Nonna, you told Lena your father went in to see Danny for the first time.
response: “My dad went in today,” he whispers. “First time.”
“First time since —?”
“Ever.”
The screen door, very quietly, as she leans back against it. “Tell me.”

So he tells her. The radio quitting in the middle of a man’s sentence when his father turned the key. The Browns hat folded in half and put inside his coat. *Where do I stand?*, between the two steel doors, low, so the girls wouldn’t hear, and Ma not turning around. Danny standing up. *They play Oakland at four. — They’ll lose. — They won’t.* The coffee with cream and two sugars, the way Danny took it at fifteen, and Danny drinking it black now, and drinking this one anyway. *It’s good, Pop.* His father’s hand out across the bolted table at the end, and Danny looking at it, and taking it.
She doesn’t say anything clever. She doesn’t say anything at all until he’s finished, and not for a little after that either, with the house going on behind her.
“And Danny drank it.”
“Yeah.”
“Of course he did.”

choices.text: “We went to see my brother. All of us.”
choices.key: Holy Family Sunday, whispering so you wouldn’t wake Nonna, you told Lena the whole family went to see Danny.
response: “We went to see my brother,” he whispers. “All of us.”
“Rosie too?”

“Rosie said grace.” He does it for her the way Rosie did it, fast, a week of practice in the bathroom mirror behind it — *bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, and Danny, and Nonna’s hand* — and leaves off the end.
“What did y’all eat?”
“Honey buns. Out of a machine. Ma dealt out paper napkins from home like it was Thanksgiving.”

“Your mama is a saint and I will hear nothing else.” She asks the right small things after that — was it warm in there, did Gina behave, did Danny laugh — and he says yes, and no, and yes. He leaves his father out of it.

choices.text: “My brother laughed at my love life till a guard looked over.”
choices.key: Holy Family Sunday, whispering so you wouldn’t wake Nonna, you told Lena your brother laughed at your love life till a guard looked over.
response: “My brother laughed at my love life,” he whispers, “till a guard looked over.”
“Your *love* life.”
“What there is of it.”
The screen door; a breath on the steps. “I’d pay to see that guard.”
“He had a newspaper. He put it down.”

“Good for him. Somebody in that room had sense.” And she wants to know what they ate, and did Rosie go, and he tells her the honey buns and the paper napkins Ma brought from home, and leaves the rest where it is.

choices.key: Holy Family Sunday, whispering so you wouldn’t wake Nonna, you told Lena your Sunday was fine. Long.
response: “Fine,” he whispers. “Long.”
“Fine,” she whispers, the way you put something back on a shelf. He hears the cup come up off the step, and go down again.

“Well,” she says. “Ours was long too.” And she tells him about the Dome instead: Remy’s face paint coming off on the man in front of him in the fourth quarter, the man turning around to say something and seeing Remy’s face and deciding against it.

body: After that it’s the warm part, and none of it matters, and it goes on past midnight. She has the 8-Ball on the step beside her — she brought it out with the coffee — and she asks it whether the Saints are resting, and he hears the blue water go around in it and the wait while the answer floats up out of the dark.
“*Signs point to yes*,” she whispers.
“It always agrees with you.”
“It knows who has custody.”

She whispers him what Mémère has already decided about New Year’s, which came down at supper and is final. Black-eyed peas and cabbage on the first, peas for luck and cabbage for money, and everybody eats both, Lucille in spirit. No sweeping on New Year’s Day, or you sweep the luck out the front door. Every light in the house on at midnight, so the year can find the place. And Remy is not to be handed anything that lights.
“That last one’s Mama’s,” Lena says. “Mémère just nodded.”

And if Minnesota loses tomorrow night, she tells him, they get home field anyway, resting or not, so Daddy has announced he’ll be praying for the Chicago Bears. “He has never prayed for the Bears in his life. He doesn’t know how. He asked me what you say to God about Chicago.”
“What’d you tell him?”
“I told him the truth. Nobody knows.”
Across the rug Nonna turns over in her chair, as far as a chair allows, and says something into the wing of it, low and clear, in Calabrese.
“*Antò. Statti zitto.*”
Then she’s breathing again, slow, the long way out.
“What did she say?” Lena whispers.
“I don’t know.”
“Liar.”
He tells her about the program in the garage, the Browns and the Colts in 1964, hung up in a freezer bag with the thumbtacks through the corners of the bag so they won’t touch it.
“In a *freezer bag*,” Lena says. “Your daddy is a romantic.”
“Don’t tell him.”

“Who would I tell? Mémère?” Somewhere on Dupre Street a car goes by slow, and she waits for it to pass, as if it could hear. “Daddy sat in his seat after the kick till they turned the field lights down. He does that when they lose. He says you don’t walk out in the middle of a funeral.”
“Have you still got my tin?” she says.
“In the Carhartt.”
“Count them.”
“I counted them Christmas Eve.”

“Count them again. I’m not asking for me. I’m asking for the tin.” He gets up off the rug without a sound, more or less, and finds the Carhartt on the hook in the hall, and comes back with the tin, and opens it in the tree light on his knee and counts them with one finger so she can hear the filters tick against the lid.
“Eleven.”
“Eleven,” she says. “Don’t you smoke one up there without me. It doesn’t count in Ohio. It’s just smoking.”

By half past twelve his ear is hot from the phone and his legs have gone to sleep on the rug, and he doesn’t move either one. They do the rest of the hour on nothing. Josie gave Remy a purple Snuggie for Christmas as a joke, and he hasn’t taken it off since, and wore it to the game under his jersey. Whether three straight in December is a sign or a cruelty: a cruelty, she says; he says a sign. Whether the bathtub Madonna in the side yard minds the snow on her shoulders. (She doesn’t, Lena rules. She’s from Nazareth. She’s just never seen it.)
At two minutes to one by the RAZR she stops in the middle of nothing.
“I have to go,” she whispers. “Julian calls at ten his time.”

body.text: Before she goes: “Tell your daddy —” and she stops. “No. Don’t tell him anything. I’m just glad.”

body: “Goodnight, Jack.”
She hangs up first.

He sits on the rug in the light off the tree with the phone shut in his hand. Four feet away his grandmother breathes in, and out, a long way out. The furnace has quit under the floor, and the ornaments on the low branches have stopped turning.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy.

body: At ten past three he’s on the front porch tying the flattened boxes from Christmas into bundles for the curb, his breath going up, the twine cutting into his fingers through the gloves, when his pocket goes.

body.text: Daddy is praying for the Bears tonight. Out loud. In the market. A man buying oysters asked him to stop. —L.

body: He carries the bundles down to the curb two at a time and stands them against the cans. The street has the week-after-Christmas quiet on it in the middle of a Monday afternoon: every driveway salted, a kid two doors up trying out a new sled on a lawn with no hill in it.

By four the front room is dark except for the tree. Through the kitchen doorway the little set at the end of the counter is on low, and the President is on it, from Hawaii, standing at a podium, talking about the man on the plane on Christmas Day. The sound is too far down to follow from the couch. Jack gets *passengers*, and *a review*, and not much else. At the kitchen table his father watches it to the end with his coffee going cold in front of him, and when they cut back to the studio he has one thing to say about it.
“They let him on the plane.”
In her chair by the window Nonna has had the beads out since three. She looks across the room at Jack over them.
“Giacomino. *Il rosario.*”

She has been asking him that since he was small enough to sit on the hassock beside her chair with his feet not reaching the rug, and in all that time he hasn’t found a reason good enough to say no to her. The hassock is the same hassock, the vinyl split along one seam and taped. His knees come up nearly to his chest on it now. Danny had it first, till he got too big and too fast at the Hail Mary, and Nonna moved him to the couch and put Jack on it, six years old, and taught him the Joyful from the Sorrowful by the days of the week. Gina is at Kelsey’s and Ma is next door at the Kovacs’ with a plate, so it’s the two of them and the tree, and that suits Nonna.

She digs in the pocket of her housedress and comes up with his: the white plastic one from his First Communion, glow-in-the-dark once, that hasn’t glowed since about 1999. She has kept it in that pocket for the times he’s home. She puts it in his hand and closes his fingers on it with hers.

Monday is the Joyful Mysteries. She starts with the crucifix, the sign of the cross made with it, and then the Creed — *Credo in Dio Padre onnipotente* — and Jack comes in under her in English, *I believe in God, the Father almighty*, the two of them half a syllable apart to the life everlasting, as they have always done it, neither language waiting for the other.

The intentions come next. She says them to the tree and the black window and whoever up there is listening, in Calabrese, with the Latin she learned in San Giovanni in Fiore and the English she learned at Sheet & Tube picnics mixed in wherever they fit, and Jack’s church-and-kitchen Italian follows most of it. Today is the Innocents, she says, and so first the babies — *i santi Innocenti*. After the babies, Nonno Antonio, *l’anima sua*, as always, and the forgotten souls in Purgatory, as always, and then:
“*Per Danny.*”
A bead. “*Per Francesco*” — she stops on the next word, and gets it right — “*che è entrato.*”
Who went in. Jack didn’t tell her. Ma must have.
“*Per la suora.*” The beads go on. “*E per Cassidy.*”
“Her name’s Skye, Nonna.”
“Cassidy,” Nonna says, and goes on to the Our Father.
He looks down at the plastic beads in his hand and follows her into it.

Through the doorway the set has moved on to the weather, a map of the Valley gone blue for Wednesday. His father turns it off. Nonna holds up the first of the ten beads between her thumb and the side of her finger, the splint resting on the arm of the chair, and looks at him to see if he’s ready.
“*Il primo mistero gaudioso*,” she says. “*L’annunciazione.*”

choices.key: On the Feast of the Holy Innocents you prayed the rosary with Nonna, and led the fifth decade.
response: She takes the first four. The Annunciation, the Visitation, the Nativity, the Presentation; the Hail Mary going around in two languages, hers a half syllable ahead, his a half syllable behind, the furnace coming on under the floor and going off again.

When she gets to the end of the fourth she stops and looks at him, and he takes the fifth. “*Il quinto mistero gaudioso*,” he says, and gets the rest of it wrong, and she fixes it for him without any fuss — “*il ritrovamento di Gesù nel tempio*” — and he leads it in English and she answers in Italian. His fingers lose the count somewhere around the sixth. Her beads keep it for him.
At the end she starts the Salve Regina and he follows her through it. Then her left hand comes off the beads and onto his face, dry as paper and warm, and she knows exactly whose face it is.
“Giacomino,” she says, like she’s making sure of it.
In the kitchen doorway his father is standing with his coffee. Jack doesn’t know how long he’s been there. When Jack looks up, Frank goes back to the table and sits down.

choices.text: *Pray it beside her and let her lead.*
choices.key: On the Feast of the Holy Innocents you prayed the rosary with Nonna, and let her lead.
response: She leads all five. He answers. The Annunciation, the Visitation; the furnace coming on under the floor and going off again.

In the third decade, somewhere in the middle of the Nativity, she loses her place. Her voice stops with a bead held between her fingers, and she looks at the bead, and he waits. It takes a while. When she starts again it’s in the fourth, not quite where she left off but close enough for God, and he goes there with her. Twice more she stops, and twice more he waits, and every time she goes on, he goes on with her.
At the end the Salve Regina, all of it, and then her left hand comes off the beads and onto his face, dry as paper and warm.
In the kitchen doorway his father is standing with his coffee. Jack doesn’t know how long he’s been there. When Jack looks up, Frank goes back to the table and sits down.

choices.text: “I have to make a call, Nonna.”
choices.key: On the Feast of the Holy Innocents Nonna asked you to pray the rosary with her. You told her you had a call to make.
response: “I have to make a call, Nonna.”
He has no call to make. She nods, and the bead goes down between her fingers, and the Hail Mary starts without him.

He goes up. The plastic rosary is still in his fist on the stairs, and he puts it in his pocket. In the back bedroom, with the door open and the phone shut in his hand and no one to call, he can hear her through the floor: the Hail Marys going around by themselves, the Finding, and the Salve Regina after, slower without anyone to keep up with. He doesn’t go back down.

body: He has been up since midnight, as he was told, sitting on the edge of his bed in the back bedroom with the lamp off and the RAZR open in his hand, so that the little screen lights and goes out and lights again whenever his thumb moves. Across from him the parka is folded on Danny’s bed.

He puts the Carhartt on over his pajama pants and goes down in his socks. At the seventh stair he steps long, to the eighth, and the house never hears him. The tree is lit in the front room for Nonna, who is asleep in her chair under it with her rosary gone slack in her lap. He goes past her and through the kitchen without a light, and opens the basement door, and pulls it to behind him.

There’s no window down here worth the name, and he doesn’t pull the string on the bulb. He knows the basement in the dark: the Dell dark on its card table, Ma’s laundry baskets, the laundry sink empty. He doesn’t sit on the steps. He crosses the concrete and sits down on the floor with his back against the furnace, against the warm sheet-metal flank of it, and the heat comes through the Carhartt into his shoulders while the floor sends its chill up through the flannel of his pajama pants to meet it. The furnace is running. He can feel it in his spine.
At 1:34 the phone goes off in his hand, and he has it open before the first buzz is done.
“Hey.”

“Hi.” Her voice is low and close, with something soft over it — a blanket, from the sound. “I’m in my childhood bed. It’s a twin. There’s a corkboard over it with every call sheet from the year I was twelve, and the print ad from the hamburger thing, so I’m being watched by me in a paper hat. My mother is at a network thing in Burbank until God knows. The parrot’s asleep under a towel. I have the entire apartment to myself and I’m lying in the bed I had braces in.” The springs go: she has turned over, or settled. “You owe me a five-day.”
“There’s no window down here.”
“Did I ask about a window? You’ve lived there your entire life. Do it from memory.” A rustle. “And use your hand. I can hear it when you don’t use your hand.”
He puts his free hand out into the dark toward the Dell, where a map would be.
“Tuesday,” he says. “Cold. Gray all day, a high just under freezing, flurries off the lake by noon. Salt trucks on Market Street by two.”
“Better. Wednesday.”
“Colder.”
“Colder isn’t a forecast. Colder is a mood.”
“Wednesday, a lot colder. Car doors frozen shut. My father out in the driveway with a kettle.”
“Thursday.”
“A full moon. Second one this month, so it’s a blue moon.”
“Is it blue?”
“No. It’s just extra.”
“That’s not weather, Jack. That’s astronomy.”
“Ask anybody with a boat.”
“Friday.”
“Friday’s yours. The Rose Bowl. Pasadena, sunny and seventy, Ohio State and Oregon, and every man on Glenwood Avenue yelling at a quarterback in California who can’t hear him.”
“Seventy is generous. Saturday.”
“Saturday, flurries. The tree stays up. My grandmother says it comes down after the Epiphany, and in this house what she says about a tree is final.”
“You did the hand for Wednesday and then you quit on the hand.”
“You can’t see my hand.”
“I can *hear* it,” Skye says. “Seven. The moon carried you.”
Under the blanket in Studio City a page turns. He knows that sound; he’d know it in his sleep.

“I have forty pages left,” she says, “and I’m not reading them, because then he stops talking. Your guy’s a dancer. He does the entire book on one foot and never falls over. It’s infuriating. Every time I think I’ve caught him at something he’s already in the next room, eating.”
“He’d like that you said that.”

“He’d make a joke about my weight.” Another page. “The fairy-tale chapter. The palace — gold, sapphire, the works. You get to live in it forever, and the one condition is there’s a word you can’t say. And out of every word in English, Jack. Out of every single one. He picked *cow*.”
“It’s a good word.”

“It’s the *perfect* word. It’s the funniest word in the language and he knew it, and he put it in the middle of the most beautiful thing in the book like a whoopee cushion on a throne.” The blanket moves. When she goes on, she’s lower. “Here’s what he gets wrong, though. He thinks the condition is the price. You pay it, you keep the palace. But you don’t even want the palace till somebody tells you there’s a word you can’t say. The no is what makes you want it.”
He turns that over against the warm metal, with the floor coming up through him.
“It’s the shape of the gift,” he says. “The condition. A palace has doors. That’s part of it being a palace.”
“You’re describing me,” Skye says.
He doesn’t have an answer to that which isn’t her name.

body.text: “And you owe me a *who*,” she says. “Saturday it was a promise. A promise to *who*. I said Monday. It’s Monday.”
“To whoever gave her the dress,” he says. “The one who wants her home.”
“So she isn’t running back to the prince.”
“The prince is the one who goes out looking.”
The mattress gives. “That’s a whole theology,” Skye says, “and you did it with a shoe.”

body: “So,” Skye says. “No questions tonight. I’m not going to ask you one thing. No cow.”
The bed takes her weight differently; he hears her settle into it, the springs and then nothing.
“Monday,” Skye says. “Not asking. Telling.”

response: “Then tell me.”
A breath on her end, close to the phone. She begins.
“It’s Tuesday here.”
“Then you’re late,” Skye says. “You’re three hours late, Costigan, and I’ve been lying here the entire time getting ready.”
She begins.
He doesn’t say anything.
Behind him the furnace goes on with its work. On her end the bed creaks and goes still, and she waits out his nothing, and then she starts.

body: Where comes first, and it comes in a voice, singsong and pleased with itself, a babysitter’s voice for a kid who won’t go down: “Once upon a time,” Skye says, “in a little room in Studio City, under a corkboard, on a twin bed —” and stops herself. “No. God, no. Not here. My mother would *know*. She’d know from the carpet.” The blanket moves. “The Saab. The turnout by the Marine Lab, top up, engine off, and the windows gone white, so there’s no ocean and no road and no anybody. Just the inside of my car. That’s where.” The springs. “And it’s the night you don’t say no. I’m not asking which night. I’m telling you what happens on it.”

“You come down past the chain in that coat, and you knock on my window like it’s a front door and somebody’s mother might answer. I lean across and open it. You get in. You’re cold, and you smell like that coat, and you don’t get to say anything; you used up all your talking in December. I take the coat first.”

She tells him the order. The Carhartt, off his shoulders and down his arms, and she’ll keep his arms caught in the sleeves longer than he likes, on purpose. His shirt next, up over his head, slow, so it catches on his ears and he has to sit there in the dark with his arms up and his face in it while she looks at him. Then she tells him what stays.

“The medal stays. I’m leaving it on you.” Her voice has come down under the blanket with her. “I’ve thought about that more than I should. How cold it is when it touches me first. How it goes warm if you wait.”
Under his T-shirt his own medal lies against his breastbone, where it has lain since his confirmation. He hasn’t thought about it in days. He can feel exactly where it is now.

“And you’re doing the clasp. I’m not helping. I’m going to lie back against the door with my arms up and let you lose to it for as long as it takes.” There’ll be static, she says. There is always static in that car. It’ll be in her hair, and when her hair comes down over him it’ll crackle, and she wants him to hear it.
“I’m keeping the anklet. That’s all I’m keeping. Everything else is yours to deal with.”

“Also I’m going to hit my knee on the gearshift. I want that known now. I hit it every single time, and I’m going to hit it then, and I’m going to swear, and you’re going to laugh at me, and I’m going to let you, once.” He laughs now, on the floor, with no sound, and on her end he hears her hear it.

Behind him the furnace shuts off. In the quiet he can hear his own breathing, and hers, and under hers the springs of a twin bed in Studio City when somebody turns over on it. He’s hard. He has been since she said *the turnout*, and there is nothing on a basement floor to be done about that, and nobody to hide it from but the furnace.
Here is where he could stop her.

He doesn’t. He can’t say yes. He has never been able to say yes to her — not on her floor, not in the Saab with the windows white, not on the bluff with no moon — and he can’t say it tonight, and under all of it he knows he won’t be able to say it in January either. So he doesn’t stop her. He lets it go on, and on, because this is the only yes there is.
“I’m going to say your name,” Skye says. “Not all of it. Just Jack. Once when I’ve got you down to the medal, like I’m checking it’s really you. And once after that. You’ll know when.”

She tells him what else she’ll say, and when. *Slower*, when he isn’t. *Look at me*, when he doesn’t. *Eyes open*, when he starts to close them. And at the very end, low, all of it — *Jack Costigan* — like a name she has been practicing for weeks to get right.

She starts at the medal. She tells him she’s going to kiss the skin under it first, and then the chain, and then go down the middle of him slowly, talking the whole way, so he can’t pretend he doesn’t know where she’s going. And when she gets there, she says, she’s going to take her time about it, and look up at him while she does, and not hurry for anything he says or any noise he makes.
His head goes back against the sheet metal. It rings, faintly, a dull note somewhere inside the furnace, and he holds still till it stops.

“And then,” Skye says, and he hears her take the breath for it, “I’m going to get on top of you, and take you inside me. Slowly. So slow you’ll think I’ve changed my mind. I won’t have. And when I have all of you I’m going to stop, and not move, and make you stay there with me and not move either, and look at you. I’ve never seen your face with the no gone out of it. I want to see it before I let you do one thing about it.”
He shuts his eyes. It doesn’t help. It’s worse: behind them is the Saab with the windows white and her in it, saying exactly that. He opens them again on the dark of the basement.

She tells him the rest. How she’ll move, and how slowly, and for how long, and when she’ll stop being slow. That the windows will run. That she’ll take his hands and put them where she wants them and leave them there. That she isn’t going to be quiet and doesn’t intend to try, and that by then she will have forgiven the gearshift everything. She tells it exact and in order, like directions to a house he’ll have to find in the dark, and every few sentences she stops to breathe, and he hears the breath go in.

“And after,” she says, barely above a whisper now, “I’m going to lie on you with my ear on your chest so I can hear it come down. And you’re going to want to say something Catholic, and I’m going to let you. And then you’re going to tell me something true. Not something nice. Something true.” The blanket moves. “And then I’m going to fall asleep on you. In a car. With my knee hurting. And you’re going to have to stay awake and keep the heater going and watch the windows clear.”

Somewhere in it his hand has gone flat on the concrete beside him, spread, the chill of the floor in his palm. The furnace lights again at his back, and the metal warms through the Carhartt, and he is sweating in a basement in December with the phone slick against his ear. Over his head the refrigerator kicks on in the kitchen, and he goes still against the furnace like somebody might come down the stairs.
“Your turn,” Skye says.

He has never said any of it to anybody. Not to her; not to himself in the dark, in so many words. He doesn’t know how to say most of it in any language but the one she has been speaking for the last half hour, and that one is hers.

choices.text: *Tell her plainly, the way she taught you.*
choices.key: On the phone in the basement at two in the morning, Skye asked for yours. You told her — plainly.
response: He tells her. He does it in sentences his father could have built, short ones, the verbs out front and the nouns coming last and late, because the nouns are the hard part. That he’d turn the engine off himself, so it was him who did it. That he’d want the dome light on; he’d want to see her. That he’d take her flannel off a button at a time and not hurry, and she’d have to let him not hurry. That when she got on top of him the way she said, he’d keep his eyes open, he wouldn’t close them, he’d — and he loses the end of it, and has to go back for it, and brings it back in the wrong order.
She’s quiet for all of it; he can hear her breathing, and the blanket when she moves. When he stops, she says, “*There* he is.”
“You’re terrible at this,” Skye says, and she’s laughing, low, with her mouth right against the phone. “Keep going.”
And he does.

body: By twenty past three his socks have gone cold through, and the furnace has shut off and lit again more times than he has counted, and the phone is hot against his ear. He moves it to the other ear. When he looks, the little screen says 1:54 on the call timer, and under that the battery is down to one bar, and he doesn’t look at that long.

She’s telling him about the drive back down afterward — the heater on their feet, the top still up, her hand on the gearshift and his over it — and he is laughing at something, quietly, with his hand over his mouth, two floors under his sleeping family.
“What’s your face doing,” she says. “Right now. Be honest.”
“I don’t know. It’s dark.”
“Feel it.”
He puts his free hand up to it. “Smiling. I think.”

“Good. Mine too. I’d hate to be doing this by myself.” She can see the ad from where she’s lying, she says — twelve years old in a paper hat, holding up a cheeseburger like an Oscar — and it is the least romantic object in the San Fernando Valley, and she has been staring it in the eye for two hours. He laughs so hard he has to press the phone against his chest till he can stop.

And it’s there, on the floor, with his face still sore from it, that he sees it. He sees all of it at once, from above, like a road on a map: this is going to make the real yes easier. Every word of tonight is in him now. The next time she’s in front of him with the windows white, none of it will be the first time he’s said it. He sees it too late to do anything but see it. And in the same breath he needs it — now, here, this — and it’s like being sick, weak with it and powerless, as if a man on a basement floor in his socks had exactly one thing left in the world he could possibly do, and he’s doing it.

On the line she’s asking him for one more thing. Not *that*, she says. Anything. So he tells her about the stairs: that one of them tells the house on you every time, that it has told on every Costigan who ever tried it, and that tonight he stepped over it.
“You snuck out,” Skye says. “To your own basement.”
“Yes.”
“For me.”
“Yes.”
She laughs, and stops in the middle of the laugh. The bed moves; the phone is closer.
“I’ve never said it before,” Skye says. “Any of it. I’ve only ever done it.”
Under its towel the parrot shifts on its perch; he can hear the wood creak.
“Saying it is worse,” she says. “It’s —”
She doesn’t finish. At his back the furnace lights, and the warmth comes up along his spine, and he waits with her.
And then she’s right back, quick and bright and on top of it: “Don’t tell anyone I said *worse*. I have a reputation.”

response: “I’ve never said any of that out loud,” he says. “To anybody.”
“I know,” Skye says. “I could tell. That was my favorite part.” The blanket. “Don’t get better at it too fast.”

response: “Tell the parrot it didn’t hear anything.”
“The parrot heard *everything*,” Skye says. “It’s LA. It’ll have a therapist by Friday. It’ll have a *book deal*.”

response: “Stay on a while,” he says. “Don’t say anything.”

She does. Her breath, close. The bed when she shifts. A long way off, a car going by on Ventura with its windows down in December, because it’s Los Angeles and it can. He sits with the phone against his ear and listens to her be there.

body: At 3:41 she starts to say goodnight.
She takes her time with it. “Go to bed,” she says. “Go up your stairs, and get in your twin bed under your crucifix, and I’m going to lie here under my hamburger and think about —”
The phone dies in his hand.
No beep. Nothing. The screen goes black in the middle of her sentence, and what he’s holding against his ear is only the weight of a phone.

He says her name into it anyway. He opens it and shuts it and holds down the red key and gets nothing back. The battery is done. The charger is upstairs on the counter by the bread box, and between him and it are the stairs and the kitchen and his family asleep.
He keeps it at his ear after that, for longer than makes any sense, the dead plastic warm against his cheek, as if she might come back out of it partway through the word.

It passes. Not all at once; a little while after. The furnace cuts out behind him, and in the quiet the sheet metal at his back gives up its heat a little at a time, and he feels it go. His breath comes down. His body comes back to being what it is the rest of the day: a body on a concrete floor in socks gone cold, with pins and needles in one foot from how he’s been sitting.

And then, with it gone, his hands start to shake. Not much. He can’t see them in the dark, but he can feel it. The dead phone is still warm, warm as something alive, and he holds it in his fist against his knee and can’t make his fingers let go of it. He can’t make himself get up yet, either, and go up those stairs and through the kitchen and past his grandmother asleep under the tree. Two hours and seven minutes. He said all of it. He would have kept on saying it. What stopped it was a battery.

It comes to him there on the floor that he is afraid, and of whom. Of himself. Of the voice that came out of him for the last hour and more, saying those things to a girl in California in his parents’ basement with his grandmother asleep over his head — and of how much he liked the sound of it.

*Be careful, Costigan.* Theo, at the side door on Christmas night, with the rain coming off the gutter behind him. *Of what?* *All of it.* At the time it sounded like Theo being Theo. On the basement floor he hears it the way it was said.
He gets as far as his knees, one hand on the furnace’s cooling side, and stops there. He doesn’t pray. He stays on his knees on the concrete, as far up as he’s got.
Over his head the house sleeps on, every room of it, the way it slept through the last two hours.
When he shifts against the furnace, the corner of the Altoids tin in the Carhartt’s pocket finds his hip.

choices.text: *Go up. Say the rosary in the dark.*

response: He goes up. The stairs; the kitchen, where he puts the dead phone on its cord by the bread box; the tree, and Nonna under it, who doesn’t stir. In the back bedroom he lies down in the Carhartt on top of the covers and starts the rosary on his fingers in the dark. It’s Tuesday, so the Sorrowful. He gets as far as the second decade and loses count, and starts that one over, and somewhere in the third he puts her in it — Skye, by name, the whole of her — and keeps going to the end.

response: He goes up the basement steps and across the kitchen in the dark, and leaves the phone on its cord by the bread box on his way, and goes out the side door. The spring yanks the door out of his fingers and bangs it shut behind him hard enough for the whole street. No light comes on upstairs.

The pack is in the Carhartt’s other pocket — his own, crushed flat, three left — not the tin. He gets one lit on the third match with his back to the house. The side yard is old snow gone hard as a sidewalk, and the Madonna stands in her tub at the back of it under his father’s blue lights. He smokes it down to the filter looking at her, and doesn’t feel any better, and didn’t expect to.

response: He sits back down against it, and stays. It takes a long time, and he doesn’t count it. The chill comes up out of the concrete into him and he sits there in it with the dead phone in his fist. When the burner finally catches behind him with its soft whump, the sheet metal warms against his back by degrees, and when he can feel it through the Carhartt he gets up, and goes up, and plugs the phone in by the bread box without turning on a light.

response: He goes up long enough to put the phone on its cord by the bread box, and comes back down to the card table. The Dell wakes up grinding. The screen comes up blue, and he signs in, and goes to her page.

Only what anybody can see: the red carpet, the boat off Catalina, her bare feet on the hood of the Saab — the ones his family passed around the kitchen table on Christmas morning. He goes through them, and through them again, and back to the first, and can’t stop. There’s no window to tell him when it gets light. The house tells him instead: the pipes knocking, the furnace, and at six-thirty, through the floor over his head, his mother’s alarm.

Frank is behind the *Vindicator*, folded to the Browns. Nonna is in her chair in the kitchen doorway, where Frank carried it after breakfast, with her coffee on the floor beside her and her eyes on everybody. At the far end of the table Rosie has the markers open in their tin and is drawing something for an envelope with a great deal of brown in it, and Gina is across from his place with a pad of lined paper and a pen, writing to Danny, her left arm curled around the page so the page stays hers.

body: Jack smiles at the kitchen table, at a plate of eggs, before he can get his face to do anything else.

At the stove his mother sees it. She turns the eggs over in the pan, one and then the other, and keeps her back to the table. Across the table Gina sees her mother see it, and puts her pen down, and picks it up again.
He shuts the phone and puts it in his pocket and picks up the fork. The coffee has gone warm enough to drink, and he drinks it.

“That’s Danny,” Rosie says, turning her drawing around for him to look at: a man in blue as tall as the page, and behind him a Christmas tree taped to a wall, and a lot of quarters. “That’s the tree that’s paper.”
“That’s good, Ro.”
“I know.” She turns it back around to add more quarters.
“Ro, he can’t have markers,” Gina says, without looking up. “It’s a letter. Not a mural.”
“He can have *pictures*.”
“He can have pictures,” Ma says from the stove, and that settles it; Rosie gets out the gray for the fence.
Gina has stopped writing. She is frowning at the page.
“How do you spell *yacht*?”
“Y-A-C-H-T.”
“*Cosa?*” Nonna says from the doorway.
“*Una barca*, Nonna,” Gina says. “A big one.”
“*Ah.*” Nonna takes this in, and takes a sip of her coffee, and looks at Jack.

Gina looks at what she’s written, and at him, and at what she’s written. “That’s not a word. That’s a *sneeze*.” She writes it anyway, a letter at a time with her tongue in the corner of her mouth, and crosses out whatever was there before it, and goes on under her breath as she writes: *on a* … *yacht* … *in a bathing suit, Ma says underwear, it is NOT underwear* … — and behind the *Vindicator* his father turns a page to the box scores.
Gina looks up at him over the pad.
“Anything you want me to tell him?”
