Gina writes it word for word, including the *no*.
“Tell him it’s a boat.”
“It’s a *yacht*, Jack.” She underlines it twice, so Danny will know she spelled it right.
“Tell him thanks for Sunday.”
Gina looks up from the pad. At the stove the spatula stops for a second, and goes on.
Gina writes it at the bottom of the page, by itself, under everything else.

s09a.slug: TUESDAY · 5:40 PM · THE SILVERADO, A SUPERMARKET LOT ON MARKET STREET
body: It’s been dark since five. The lot lights have come on orange over the slush, and the Silverado sits under one of them two rows back from the cart corral, engine running for the heater. Ma’s list is on the dash in her school-office capitals — MILK, ITALIAN BREAD, EGGS (LARGE) — and under it, in his father’s pencil, 2 TICKETS. Jack hasn’t gone in yet. Across the lot the doors keep opening on the bright inside of the store and letting people out with New Year’s in their carts, cases of pop, sleeves of plastic cups, a woman with three heads of cabbage in her arms like she’s carrying a baby.
At twenty to six the RAZR goes on the seat beside him. LENA.
“Home field,” she says, before he’s got it all the way to his ear.
“What?”
“*Home field.* Chicago beat the Vikings in overtime last night, so it comes through the Dome the whole way. Every game till Miami. Resting was *strategy*. Tell your daddy.”

He has never seen Broussard’s Seafood. He has it built anyway, out of four months of her talking: the long white cases of ice, the prices in grease pencil on the glass, her father’s Saints calendar over the register with the games crossed off in red. Behind her now it’s that, on Banks Street, the week after Christmas. The ice machine lets go of a load into its bin with a crash. A woman wants four dozen oysters for New Year’s and wants them big. Somewhere back of the register a radio is playing a record older than his father, a man singing the blues in a girl’s voice and then, for no reason anybody ever explained, a frog’s.

“I’m on the register,” she says. “I’m always on the register this week, every year since I could reach the drawer. Luc did it before me, and Remy did it for one afternoon in 2004, and we don’t talk about that afternoon. Four dozen, ma’am? Large? Yes, ma’am. Daddy, four dozen large.”

Then, to somebody on her end, at full Broussard volume: “Mr. Duplantier, I am not selling you shrimp at that price, I don’t care if you held me at my baptism. You dropped me at my baptism. Mama has pictures.” A man’s voice, aggrieved, and Tony’s from further back telling him to pay the girl. “Thank you, Mr. Duplantier. Happy New Year. Kiss Miss Rita.” And back into the phone, ordinary: “What is that noise?”
“My dad’s truck. I’m in a parking lot with my mother’s list.”
“Read it to me.”
He reads it to her off the dash. Milk. Italian bread. Eggs, large. Two tickets.
“*Italian* bread,” Lena says. “Y’all are lost up there. What tickets?”
“Lottery. My dad. Every Tuesday.”

“Tell him I said play the birthdays. Daddy plays all of ours and Mémère’s and Drew Brees’s, and he’s never won a dime, and he says that’s how you know it’s honest.” The register drawer rings open and shut. “He was in here at seven this morning lighting a candle in his head for a man named Jay Cutler. He wants to send him a sack of crawfish when they’re in season. He wants to know does Chicago have an address.” The ice machine. “Last night he watched it in the back office on the little TV with the foil on the antenna, and when Chicago scored in overtime he kissed the screen. On the mouth. Mémère saw. She hasn’t said a word to him since and it’s the happiest I’ve seen her all week.”
“The radio says Wednesday’s the coldest day of the year.”
“Colder than *now*? Jack. You’ll die. Wear the jacket. Wear two of the jacket.”
“We won Sunday,” Jack says. “Three straight.”
“Three.” She doesn’t sound one bit impressed, and she sounds pleased for him anyway. “Lord. Cleveland’s going to be impossible.”
Then a man’s voice comes up behind her, big enough to fill the market. “Is that the Ohio boy?”
“It’s the Ohio boy.”
“Tell him New Orleans is *resting*!”
“He heard you, Daddy. Algiers heard you.”

“And tell him —” closer now, right at her shoulder, cheerful, a man with nothing on his mind but a pot — “tell him I got a gumbo going for the musician Wednesday. *Real* one. Not that restaurant mess.”
“*Daddy.*”
“What? He’s a nice boy.”

Out in the lot a woman pushes a cart past the Silverado’s grille with a little boy riding in the basket, both of them in Steelers hats. The heater ticks. A plow goes by out on Market Street, and its orange light turns once across the dash and the list and is gone.
“Julian lands tomorrow at four,” Lena says. “Daddy’s taking him to the market first. To see the shrimp.”
The ice machine lets go of another load.
“I won’t call as much this week.”
“I know.”
On her end, a breath, and the register drawer, and the man on the record still going.
“…I’ll call.”

choices.text: “Tell your father the Browns are resting too.”
response: “Tell your father the Browns are resting too.”
She doesn’t have to. Tony has heard it from across the market. “*Lord*, son.” The oyster woman laughs, and Lena says she has a customer, and goes.
He sits in the lot with the list until the windshield fogs.
“Save me an oyster.”
“They don’t keep, Jack.”
“Then eat one for me.”
“I’ll eat *two*,” Lena says, and goes back to the four dozen.
He sits in the lot with the list until the windshield fogs.
“Go sell your shrimp, Broussard.”
“Yes, sir.” She’s gone on it, laughing at something the oyster woman said.
He sits in the lot with the list until the windshield fogs.

body: The cold came down out of Canada on Tuesday night and sat on the Valley, and by Wednesday morning it has its hand on everything: the storm door frozen to its frame until Ma put her hip into it, the salt on the walk squeaking under a boot, the Silverado dead in the drive. In the garage the space heater is going full out at Frank’s feet, and it makes a circle about three feet across where a man can stand and not see his breath. Outside the circle he can.

The truck’s battery is up on the workbench on the trickle charger, clamps on, the needle hardly moving. Beside it on the bench is Frank’s old phone, which spent the night on the seat of the truck and is as dead as the battery.
“Cold got ’em both,” Frank says. “Same night.”

Jack brought out the coffee Ma sent and has been holding the trouble light since, over the engine while his father did the terminals with a wire brush and a paste of baking soda, and then over the bench, where there’s nothing left to light. “Battery’s from ’04,” Frank said, about an hour ago. “Owes me nothing.” At ten past ten his father looks up at the clock over the pegboard, the one that has said GENUINE CHEVROLET PARTS since before Jack was born, and holds out his hand.
“Give me yours.”
“Who are you calling?”
“The hall. They’re doing the list over. Small car.” Frank takes the RAZR and opens it like it might go off. “You call, you give your name, you give your years. Spring, maybe.”

He dials from a card out of his wallet, one thick finger, one number at a time, checking the card between each. Then he stands in the heater’s circle with his son’s phone held a little off his ear, the way he holds every phone that isn’t the kitchen’s, and waits. Jack can hear the hold music from where he is: a saxophone doing something to a song he almost knows. Frank looks at the battery. The battery looks back.
“How long do they keep you?”

“Long as they want.” Frank shifts the phone to the other ear, and has to look for where on it the ear goes. “Used to be you stood in line at the hall. In the snow. Now you stand in your garage and they play you a song.”
Eleven minutes. The saxophone goes around twice.
At 10:22 the RAZR beeps in his father’s ear. Twice.
Jack has had the phone since August and he knows those two beeps. They’re for a message, any message — Kevin, Gina, the phone company — and his stomach knows that too and doesn’t care.

Frank takes it down. He holds it out at arm’s length, open, and squints at the inside screen, and his face does nothing at all. Then he shuts it — which hangs up on the hall, eleven minutes and the saxophone — and holds it out to Jack, shut.
“You got a picture.”

Jack takes it. His father picks his own dead phone up off the bench and puts it in his coat pocket, for no reason Jack can see, and goes out the side door of the garage and across the drive to start over on the kitchen phone. Not a word about the eleven minutes.

On the outer screen, the little envelope. Inside, two messages at the top of the list, one with the picture icon beside it. Through the kitchen window across the drive his father has the wall phone already and is dialing again with the card held up to the light.

s10a.slug: THURSDAY · 7:38 AM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE, THE STEPS
body: Wednesday nothing came from New Orleans — not a text, all day, the first day since he got home.

Thursday the bells go for the end of the seven o’clock at St. Brigid’s and the doors let a dozen people out into a morning just starting to go gray over the South Side. Ma has gone to the seven o’clock on the last day of the year every year since she was a girl; this year he went with her. It was Saint Sylvester, a pope from the fourth century, and Father Dom read the beginning of John with his cough drop parked in his cheek — *the light shines in the darkness* — and in the prayers of the faithful, after the sick of the parish and before the dead, he prayed for the Americans killed in Afghanistan, and for their families, and the dozen of them answered him.

On the way out she stopped at the Mary altar, as she does on this morning, and lit a candle and put a dollar through the slot, and stood there with her gloves in one hand long enough that he went and stood with her. On the steps now Ma buttons her coat to the top and goes on down to the curb to warm up the truck. A salt truck comes up the street throwing its fan of grit at the parked cars. Over the roofs to the west the moon is still up, full and low and white, in a sky that’s already day around it.
At 7:38 the RAZR goes in his coat. LENA.
“I said I’d call,” she says.

She’s on the Moonwalk by the river, on a bench, with a café au lait and a bag of beignets from across the street, and the Quarter is empty: a man hosing down the flagstones in front of the café, a street sweeper going around Jackson Square, the pigeons. “This is the only hour it belongs to New Orleans,” she says. The barges for tonight are already anchored out in the river toward Algiers, and a tug is nosing at one of them. “Everybody on Dupre Street is asleep. Julian’s asleep in Remy’s room with his shoes lined up under the bed. Remy’s on the couch. He’s furious about it.”

“I left at six,” she says. “In Remy’s sneakers, they were by the door. I left a note on the icebox so Mama wouldn’t call Luc and have the Fifth District out looking for me.” The bag rustles. “Nobody’s down here this early but pigeons and people who work here and a few crazy people. And me. I’ve been coming since high school. It’s the only time the river sounds like a river.”
Jack sits down on the top step. The stone comes straight through his good pants.

“He peeled shrimp with Daddy for two hours yesterday and never once complained,” Lena says. “Daddy says he has the hands for it.” The bag rustles. “The gumbo happened. Mémère ironed the tablecloth twice.”
He doesn’t have anything for that. On her end the river goes on, and she waits a second for him, and then doesn’t.
The salt truck has turned at the corner and is coming back down the far side of the street.
“What is that?” she says.
“Salt truck. I’m on the church steps. Ma’s in the truck with the heater going.”
“Then go get in the truck, Jack.”
“In a minute.”

“Your mama’s going to think I’m a bad influence.” A paper bag, and something she tells somebody on her end — *merci, Mr. Ngo* — and back. “The waiter brought me a second order on the house because it’s the last day of the year. He’s been bringing me second orders since I was fourteen. He says I look like I need it. I have not ever needed it.” Powdered sugar, audibly. “I eat it anyway. It would be rude.”
“What are y’all doing tonight?” she says.

“Rosie’s midnight. At nine. Off a tape. Pots and pans on the porch.” He watches the truck’s grit hit the windshields of the cars along the curb. “Then a party. A guy from high school. His mother’s basement.”

“Look at you, going out.” A ship somewhere downriver sounds its horn, long. “Mémère has us on the levee by eleven-thirty in church clothes so the year can see we tried. Daddy’s bringing the chairs. Remy’s been told about the lighting things.”

Then, for half an hour, nothing that matters. Down by the river steps a man in a Saints toboggan is practicing the trumpet, scales, up and down and wrong at the same place every time, and she holds the phone out so Jack can hear him miss it. She’s got powdered sugar on her coat and on a pigeon that came too close, she says, and she isn’t brushing any of it off, because it’s Café du Monde sugar and that’s practically a sacramental. She wants to know what the Gospel was. He tells her John, the beginning, and she says the first line back to him from memory — “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” — and a gull goes over her, loud, and she says the next — “He was in the beginning with God” — and stops there, and drinks her coffee.

“Did Rosie say grace again?” “Every meal. She’s added the Browns.”
“How’s Danny?” “Laughing at me.” “Good.”

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her.

s11.slug: THURSDAY · 9:00 PM · THE FRONT ROOM → THE PORCH
s11.music: Ella Fitzgerald — “What Are You Doing New Year’s Eve?”
body: At ten to nine the VCR under the television is rewinding with its little motor whining, and Ma has put a CD in the player on top of the console stereo to cover the sound of it, and turned the lamp off so the tree can have the room. The tape lives on top of the VCR all year in a cardboard sleeve, and the label says, in Ma’s capitals: TIMES SQ. 12-31-99 — DO NOT TAPE OVER — FRANK THIS MEANS YOU.

Rosie’s midnight is at nine. It has been at nine since Gina was small enough to fall asleep in a paper hat, and it has been this tape since the real millennium, when Frank sat up with a blank cassette in the machine and his thumb over RECORD so the kids could have it after. Jack did midnight at nine off it till he was twelve and too old for it, and then he was the one who ran the VCR. Tonight it’s Gina’s job. She has the remote in one hand and Theo’s Flip in the other, and has told everyone twice that she is shooting a documentary and nobody is to look at the camera.

Rosie is standing on the coffee table, allowed tonight and no other night of the year, in her pajamas and her church shoes, with Ma’s saucepan in one hand and a wooden spoon in the other. Nonna is in her chair by the window with her beads and a pot lid in her lap. Frank is on the couch. Ma stands in the kitchen doorway with the dish towel over her shoulder, where she can watch the tape and the stove both.

The tape clunks at the start and plays. It’s ten years ago in Times Square: a million people with their breath going up in the lights, kids on their fathers’ shoulders in novelty glasses shaped like 2000, and Dick Clark telling all of them how long they’ve got. The picture rolls once where the tape has gotten tired. Rosie doesn’t care. When the crowd on the screen starts counting she counts with it at the top of her lungs, and the front room counts along with a crowd ten years gone — Gina behind the Flip, Frank low from the couch, Ma from the doorway — and Nonna half a number behind all of them in Italian, *sette, sei, cinque*, coming in under the English, as she does at the rosary. At zero the ball comes down and the 2000 under it lights up, and 1999 throws its hats in the air, and Rosie hits the saucepan so hard the spoon flies out of her hand and into the tree.

For the porch, Ma has the pots out on the radiator by the front door, the same pots every year: the spaghetti pot and its lid, the cast-iron that only Frank can lift with one hand, two saucepans, and the colander for Gina, who likes the sound. Frank turns Nonna’s chair around to face the door and opens it wide, and Nonna sits in the cold coming in with her coat over her knees and the pot lid held up, ready. Everybody else goes out.

Glenwood is frozen hard and empty under the streetlights, and the moon is up over the roofs across the street, full, so bright the salt on the walk throws little shadows. In the side yard the Madonna stands blue in her tub under Frank’s lights. Rosie goes first, on the top step, beating the saucepan at the street, and then all of them: Ma on the spaghetti pot, Frank on the cast-iron with the spoon going like he’s mad at it, Gina on the colander with the Flip held out in her other hand, and behind them in the open door Nonna’s lid, *ding, ding, ding*, a little off the beat. Two doors up, past the Santa still lying on his face in the yard, a porch light comes on and somebody bangs back. Somebody further down the block answers on what has to be a hubcap.
“It’s a blue moon,” Gina tells Rosie between bangs. “Second full one in a month.”
Rosie stops banging to look up at it. She looks for some time. “It’s not *blue*.”
“It’s an expression.”
Rosie goes back to the saucepan, without the same heart in it.

Inside, Ma has the Asti out of the refrigerator and the little juice glasses on a tray: a finger in each for her and Nonna and Jack, a finger for Gina, who gets a look with it, and grape juice for Rosie in a real wine glass, because she asked for one in October. Frank’s is a ginger ale, in a glass. He lifts it.
“Everybody,” he says, and they drink.
Ma looks at the glass in his hand, and then at the tree, and drinks her Asti.
Gina has the Flip up again with the red light on. “The Costigan New Year Documentary,” she announces. “Resolutions. One line each. No speeches, *Ma*.”

Frank, on the couch, into the lens: “Browns.” Ma, from the doorway: “Everybody eats.” Gina swings it to the window, and Nonna leans in close to the little camera and tells it something in Calabrese, at length, with one finger up, and sits back satisfied. “I’m not translating that,” Gina says. “That’s for the extras.” Rosie, from the coffee table, with grape juice on her lip: “Another crab.”
Then the camera comes around to Jack on the end of the couch, and the little red light waits on him.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip.

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab. Rosie’s midnight is at nine, off a tape Dad made in 1999. Pots and pans on the porch. Asleep by a quarter past with the spoon.

s11a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:25 PM · A BASEMENT ON THE SOUTH SIDE
body: Ryan Pallante’s basement is knotty-pine paneling and a drop ceiling with a water stain in the shape of Ohio, a bar his father built from a kit the year Ryan was born, a dryer with a cooler of ice on top of it, and a sheet of plywood across two sawhorses for beer pong. Somebody’s iPod sits in a dock on the bar playing something with a great deal of synthesizer in it that three girls from Ursuline know every word of. There are forty people down here, and Jack went to grade school or Mooney or CYO with most of them, and the rest are somebody’s cousin. Upstairs Mrs. Pallante has a ham out on the kitchen table under foil, and every half hour she comes to the top of the stairs to tell the room there’s ham.

Ryan sees him at the bottom of the stairs and comes through the crowd with both arms up. Ryan is the boy who learned everybody’s middle name off the program at Mooney’s graduation and has used them ever since, at volume. “John *Anthony* Costigan! *California!*” He takes the pizzelles and passes them back over his shoulder to somebody, and the room turns around. “You see any movie stars out there?”
“One,” Jack says.
And the basement laughs, because it’s a joke. Ryan yells *ONE* at the drop ceiling like a final score, and somebody puts a beer in Jack’s hand.

It’s a Rolling Rock out of the cooler on the dryer, and he makes it last. Ryan himself is drinking Cherry Coke out of the can, because he has two cousins to drive home to Boardman at one o’clock, and he tells that to everybody who offers him anything, as if it’s news.

Tommy Hritz is here from St. Christine’s, the size of a refrigerator now, who broke Jack’s nose in the third quarter of the eighth-grade CYO game that Jack started. He comes over and shakes Jack’s hand like it was a long time ago, which it was, and studies the nose.
“Healed crooked.”
“You did good work.”
Tommy seems pleased with that, and goes back to the beer pong.

By the bar the Mooney kids have gotten around to Mr. Tomko, who taught them theology sophomore year, and somebody does him for Jack — the glasses pushed up on the forehead, the finger — “*Mister* Costigan. You will not out-Catholic me in my own classroom.” Jack got a detention for that one, for arguing the Pope’s side better than the textbook did, and served it, and served the six-thirty Mass the next morning anyway. Half the room calls him Costigan and the other half calls him Jack, and two girls from St. Brigid’s still call him Jackie, from the first grade, and he lets them.
Ryan’s cousin Bobby, who was a year behind Danny at Mooney and played JV with him, gets Jack by the furnace for a minute, away from the music.
“How’s Danny doing?”
“He’s good. He reads.”
Bobby nods at that. He says to tell him Bobby says hey, and that’s as far as he takes it, and they go back to the room.
Across the basement, by the beer pong, Carly Benedetto in the white knit hat catches his eye and raises her cup to him.

At eleven Mrs. Pallante comes down the stairs herself with a ham sandwich on a paper plate, and a pickle, and finds him in the crowd by the bar, and puts it in his hands. “Your mother called,” she says. “Half past nine. She says you didn’t eat.”
“I ate twice.”

“She said you’d say that.” Mrs. Pallante watches him take the first bite. Then she picks the pizzelle plate up off the dryer, empty now except for the plastic wrap, and holds it up at him. “And you tell her I don’t have her platter. I never had her platter. You tell her look in her own cupboard over the refrigerator.” And she goes back up the stairs with the plate, to the ham.

The iPod goes from the synthesizers to Springsteen and back. A girl from Latin Club wants to know if it’s true they surf at his school, before class, and is disappointed in his answer. A boy who backed him up at point guard wants him in on the next game. Somebody’s little brother came down the stairs an hour ago and ate the pizzelles off the dryer one after another, and is now asleep under the bar.

At twenty-five to twelve Mrs. Pallante has the TV in the kitchen up loud enough that Times Square comes down the stairs, and down here a girl from Boardman with a voice built for running things is going around the room with a napkin and a pen, organizing who kisses whom at midnight. She is working her way down the paneling toward his end of it.

body: At a minute to twelve Ryan puts the Killers on and turns the dock up till the bar buzzes, and the whole basement sings it at the drop ceiling with their heads back, forty people who know every word, so that when Mrs. Pallante yells down the stairs that it’s on, the countdown comes down underneath the song from the kitchen TV and they have to count over it. *Ten.* The girl from Boardman has her napkin out. *Nine.* People are finding each other across the beer pong. Somewhere around the eight Jack is through the laundry room, and at the six he’s on the back stairs, and the back door lets him out into the night at about the two. Behind it the year turns over, muffled, in forty voices and one song.
Carly Benedetto is already out here, on the top step with her coat pulled around her and her knees up, smoking. She looks up at the door, and at him, and moves over to make room.
“Happy New Year,” she says.
“Happy New Year.”
He sits. In his coat the phone goes against his ribs, and again, and a third time.
“Go ahead,” Carly says. “Everybody’s got somebody.”
He opens it. There are three from midnight, all at once.

body: Theo’s he leaves for the walk home. He shuts the phone, and puts it away, and Carly is watching the yard.
Carly holds her pack out to him, Marlboro Lights, the same as junior year.
“I quit.”
“Since when?”
“I’m tapering.”
Carly laughs with the smoke still in her and has to cough it out, and puts the pack away.
Two yards over somebody has set a fountain off in the snow, and it spits green at the dark, and then gold. The moon is so bright he can tell her breath from her smoke.
“Ryan does this every year,” she says. “Every year his mother does the ham. Every year Bobby gets sick in the laundry sink, and every year he says it was the ham.”

She’s at YSU now, living at home, with chemistry at eight in the morning from a man who calls the roll by last names. “He calls me Benedetto. Like a sergeant. I said it’s Miss Benedetto. He said not in his room it isn’t.” Her mother is asleep in the recliner in front of the TV with her rosary in her lap. “She’ll wake up at one and tell me she saw the ball. She hasn’t seen the ball since Reagan.”
“You look like California,” she says.
“Fog. The whole time.”
“Still.”

She smokes. Over their heads in the kitchen Mrs. Pallante is laughing at somebody. Carly is watching the swing set at the back of the yard, which has a ridge of snow along the top bar and a seat hanging by one chain.
“Do you ever hear how Mikey’s mom is doing?”
The fountain two yards over burns down to the cardboard and quits, and whoever lit it says *aw*. Carly has turned to look at him with the cigarette halfway to her mouth, and it stops there.
“Jack. You okay? You went white.”
His hands are on the iron rail. He takes them off it and puts them in the pockets of the Carhartt.
She looks back out at the yard. “She goes to the nine-thirty at St. Nicholas,” Carly says. “In Struthers. She sits in the back.”
Inside, the song ends, and somebody starts it over. Carly smokes the cigarette down until there’s nothing left of it but filter, and looks at the filter.
“I go sometimes,” she says. “I sit behind her.”

journal.title: Carly Benedetto
journal.text: Mooney ’09, YSU now. Two pews up at Midnight Mass with her mother. Gave me the peace. Asked me to a thing at Ryan’s on New Year’s. New Year’s at Ryan Pallante’s, his mother’s basement. After midnight she was out on the back steps with a cigarette, and so was I.

response: “No,” he says. “I don’t.”
Carly nods, like it’s the answer she came out here with, and puts the cigarette out on the rail.

She goes back in after that, and the song comes out the door with her and goes back in when it shuts. He stays out on the steps until his ears ache. At twenty to one he goes down them and around the side of the house and starts home across the South Side, under a moon bright enough to lay his shadow out on the salt ahead of him.

s12b.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 PM · THE SIDEWALKS, THE SOUTH SIDE
body: At twenty to twelve he goes up the stairs past the ham, tells Mrs. Pallante happy New Year and that his mother wants her platter, and lets himself out the front door with Ryan yelling *JOHN ANTHONY, IT’S NOT MIDNIGHT* up the stairwell after him. Carly Benedetto is on the front walk ahead of him, pulling on her gloves. She’s leaving too.
“My mother wants me home by midnight,” she says. “She’s Slovak about it.”

The Benedettos are St. Brigid’s people, two streets over from Glenwood. It’s the same walk. They take it down the middle of the sidewalk under the full moon, which is high now and so bright the parked cars have shadows, and every house they pass has its television going behind the curtains on the same channel, so that Times Square comes out of one house and goes back into the next. When a car comes along they step off onto the lawns, and the snow crust creaks under their boots.
Halfway down the first block she lights a cigarette, Marlboro Lights, the same as junior year, and holds the pack out to him.
“I quit.”
“Since when?”
“I’m tapering.”

Carly laughs with the smoke still in her and has to cough it out at the moon. She’s at YSU now, living at home, with chemistry at eight in the morning from a man who calls the roll by last names. “He calls me Benedetto. Like a sergeant. I said it’s Miss Benedetto. He said not in his room it isn’t.” Her mother was asleep in the recliner by ten with her rosary in her lap. “She’ll tell me tomorrow she saw the ball. She hasn’t seen the ball since Reagan.” And Ryan’s party is the same every year, she says: the ham, the Killers at midnight, and Bobby sick in the laundry sink by one, swearing it was the ham. “Give him an hour.”
“You look like California,” she says.
“Fog. The whole time.”
“Still.”
Up ahead, at the corner where she turns off, her mother’s porch light is on. Carly has her eyes on it.
“Do you ever hear how Mikey’s mom is doing?”
Three more steps, and then she stops on the sidewalk, because he isn’t beside her. She turns around.
“Jack? You okay? You went white.”
His hands are in the pockets of the Carhartt, as far down as they go. A block back, somebody’s storm door bangs, and a party comes out of it and goes back in.
She waits for him to come up even with her, and then she says it walking again, with her eyes up the street. “She goes to the nine-thirty at St. Nicholas. In Struthers. She sits in the back.”
At the corner Carly stops to work her glove down tighter at the wrist.
“I go sometimes,” she says. “I sit behind her.”

s12c.slug: THURSDAY · 11:58 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT ROOM
s12c.music: Guy Lombardo and His Royal Canadians — “Auld Lang Syne”
body: He comes in the side door at two minutes to twelve with the night still on his coat, and the front room is the tree and the television. Ma and his father are on the couch with Rosie asleep across both their laps, her feet on Frank and the wooden spoon still in her fist, and on the screen it’s Times Square for real this time, this year’s, with Dick Clark and Ryan Seacrest and the ball at the top of its pole. Gina is cross-legged on the rug with the Flip. Nonna is awake in her chair by the window, sitting up for it. Jack sits down on the rug beside Gina in his coat.

At a minute to, Ma gets up and turns the sound off and puts the record on the turntable in the console, as she has every year Jack can remember, the needle set down by hand, and is back on the couch before the ball starts down.

It comes down in silence, with the old band playing the old song out of the corner of the room. At zero his mother and father kiss over Rosie, quick, embarrassed by it, Frank’s hand coming up off Rosie’s ankle to Ma’s face and going straight back. Gina has the Flip on them. “*Regina*,” Ma says. “It’s *history*,” Gina says, and keeps filming, until Frank reaches over and puts his hand over the lens.

From the window Nonna says it. “*Buon anno.*” And then to each of them by name, one and the next, like beads: “Francesco. Maria. Regina. Rosaria” — who is asleep, and gets hers anyway — “Giacomino.” Then she looks past all of them at the wing chair by the stairs, where Danny watched the ball every year from the time he was old enough to stay up for the real one, and where nobody has sat tonight.
“Danny,” she says to it. “*Buon anno.*”
In his pocket the phone goes against his leg, three times, one after another, and he leaves it there till she’s done.
On the screen the year has gone up in confetti over a million people. His father watches it over Rosie’s feet.
“Twenty-ten,” Frank says. He tries it again. “Sounds like a year somebody builds a car.”

The record comes to the end of the song, and the needle runs on into the hiss. Ma gets up to see to it, and to the dishes after. Jack stays on the rug with his back against the couch and takes out the phone.

Her whole family is out there in church clothes — Mémère, and her father with the chairs, and Remy not being handed anything that lights — and Julian beside her, who has never seen it. She must have had it typed before the year came, with her thumb on the key, and she sent it before she turned to any of them.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks, before anybody. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it.

s14.slug: FRIDAY · 3:00 AM · THE BASEMENT, THE DELL
body: At five to three the basement is the furnace and the Dell. The furnace is between runs, ticking as it cools. The Dell is back on its card table by the laundry sink, its fan whining, the only light down here, and it puts his shadow up the paneling behind him the size of a door. Over his head the whole house is asleep, the year included. He came down in the Carhartt over his pajama pants with a glass of milk, because the basement is the one room in the house where a light on at this hour doesn’t climb the stairs. Ma’s laundry baskets are stacked by the sink, folded and waiting. The old Zenith is under its bedsheet. The keyboard is the family’s, with half the letters worn off the keys and a horse sticker of Gina’s from the sixth grade on the space bar, and he types on it with two fingers.
Theo’s text has been on the RAZR since midnight.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed Christmas night — they wanded the baccalà. At the side door Christmas night he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band.

He clicks it anyway, because she sent it, and the page takes its time. When it starts he does what she said. He turns the folding chair around on the concrete so his back is to the screen, and puts his sock feet up on Ma’s laundry basket, and sits facing the furnace with his hands in the pockets of the Carhartt.

It comes out of the Dell’s two little speakers thin and tinny and too loud for twenty past three, a band from somewhere playing the new year in on an organ and a lot of drums, and out in the hills, if she meant it, a girl is walking back around a pool with the same song in her ear. The furnace has a little window in its door with the pilot showing through it. He watches that, and listens to the end. When it’s over he reaches back behind him without looking and finds the mouse, and starts it again.
